name: Boots Soltan / star rating

lead: The Boots star rating is a label that helps you pick sunscreens with stronger UVA protection relative to UVB. UVA is tied to skin aging and pigmentation, so choosing more stars aims at less photoaging and more even skin.

It runs from one to five stars, with five the highest UVA ratio, and is based on a proprietary in vitro test. Brian Diffey at Newcastle University did the original work and Boots developed the method, which many UK manufacturers adopted. Soltan is a Boots sunscreen range.

paras: People look for the star mark on UK and Irish sunscreen packs and choose higher-star products for daily facial and holiday use, reading it alongside the SPF number.
The stars describe the UVA-to-UVB ratio, not total protection, so SPF still matters. Studies note labelling differences between regions and products with identical SPF.

angle.text: Users in the UK and Ireland read the star rating to pick sunscreens with stronger UVA protection relative to UVB, since UVA is tied to skin aging and pigmentation. Higher-star products aim at less photoaging and more even skin; it is a labelling method, not a product.

lead: The Boots star rating is a UK and Ireland labelling system for the UVA protection of sunscreens, expressed relative to UVB protection. Wikipedia describes it as a proprietary in vitro method in which five stars is the highest UVA ratio and one star the lowest [1]. Soltan is a sunscreen range from Boots; the sources reviewed do not describe it.
Brian Diffey at Newcastle University did the original work, and Boots in Nottingham developed the method, which many UK manufacturers adopted [1].

paras: The method compares UVA to UVB protection in vitro. After revision following the Colipa UVA PF test and updated EU recommendations, samples are pre-irradiated to better reflect in-use UVA protection, and the lowest rating became three stars [1].

Separately, EU rules require UVA protection of at least one-third of the labelled SPF to carry the UVA seal, from European Commission Recommendation 2006/647/EC [1]. SPF itself was introduced in 1974 and EU labels cap at 50+ [1].

A 2011 study of fifteen European sunscreens with the same labelled SPF found differences in photoprotection under natural sunlight, and called for global harmonisation of photostability and UVA labelling [2]. A 2008 study assessed UVA protection in vitro of 13 popular U.S. sunscreens at a time when the U.S. had no UVA testing or labelling regulation [3].
No studies found that evaluate the Boots star rating itself in people. Related laboratory work on UVA protection is cited above [2][3].

timeline.event: European Commission Recommendation 2006/647/EC sets one-third UVA rule. [1]
